cards.front: Define [[kw:face amount]] in life insurance.
back: The death benefit stated in the policy, paid to the beneficiary upon the insured's death.
Used to calculate the premium: $$\frac{\text{Face Amount}}{1{,}000} \times \text{Rate per } \$1{,}000$$
Also called face value or death benefit.
Temporary coverage for a specified period (1, 5, 10, 20, 30 years).
Cheapest form of life insurance; no cash value accumulates.
If the insured outlives the term, the policy expires with no value.
Premiums increase at renewal.
cards.front: What is [[kw:term insurance]]?

back: Permanent protection for the insured's entire life.
Higher premiums than term because part funds a [[kw:cash value]] savings component.
The premium remains level for life.
Cash value can be borrowed against or used for nonforfeiture options.
cards.front: Explain [[kw:straight life (ordinary life) insurance]].

back: Permanent coverage with premiums paid for only 20 years.
After 20 years, the policy is [[kw:paid‑up]]—no more premiums are due.
Cash value builds faster than straight life.
Lifetime protection with a limited payment period.
cards.front: What is [[kw:20‑payment life insurance]]?
List the three [[kw:nonforfeiture options]] available in permanent life insurance.
back: 1. Cash surrender – receive accumulated cash value; policy ends.
2. Reduced paid‑up insurance – use cash value to buy a smaller permanent policy with no further premiums.
3. Extended term insurance – use cash value to buy term insurance for the full face amount for a limited time.
[[imp:These options protect the policyholder's accumulated value if premiums stop.]]

cards.front: How is the annual [[kw:fire insurance premium]] calculated?
back: $$\text{Annual Premium} = \frac{\text{Face Amount}}{100} \times \text{Rate per } \$100$$
Rates are higher for frame construction than brick.
Separate policies may be needed for building and contents.
Coverage can include extended perils (wind, hail, explosion).

cards.front: A building is insured for \$200,000 at a rate of \$0.45 per \$100. Find the annual premium.
What is a [[kw:coinsurance clause]] in fire insurance?
back: Requires the insured to carry coverage equal to at least a specified percentage (usually 80%) of the property's value.
If underinsured, recovery for a partial loss is reduced proportionally.
$$\text{Amount Paid} = \frac{\text{Insurance Carried}}{\text{Insurance Required}} \times \text{Loss}$$
[[imp:Encourages insuring close to full value.]]

cards.front: Compute coinsurance payment: building worth \$400,000, insured for \$280,000, 80% clause, loss \$100,000.
back: Insured bears the remaining \$12,500.
Short‑rate (insured cancels): refund based on a penalty table; less than pro‑rata.
Pro‑rata (insurer cancels): refund = Annual premium × (Remaining months / 12); no penalty.
[[imp:Short‑rate always gives a smaller refund than pro‑rata.]]
cards.front: What is the difference between [[kw:short‑rate]] and [[kw:pro‑rata]] cancellation refunds?
Define [[kw:actual cash value (ACV)]].
back: $$\text{ACV} = \text{Replacement Cost} - \text{Depreciation}$$
Standard fire policies pay ACV unless replacement cost coverage is added.
ACV leaves a gap that replacement cost coverage can fill.
Replacement cost pays for new materials without deduction for depreciation.

cards.front: What are the three main types of auto insurance coverage?
back: [[kw:Liability]] – covers damage/injuries you cause to others (required in most states).
[[kw:Collision]] – covers damage to your own car from a crash.
[[kw:Comprehensive]] – covers non‑crash damage: theft, fire, hail, vandalism, animal strikes.
Collision and comprehensive are optional unless the car is financed.

cards.front: Explain [[kw:split liability limits]] (e.g., 100/300/50).
back: First number: max bodily injury per person (\$100,000).
Second number: max total bodily injury per accident (\$300,000).
Third number: max property damage per accident (\$50,000).
If damages exceed limits, the insured pays the excess.

cards.front: What is a [[kw:deductible]] in auto insurance and how does it affect premiums?
back: The amount the insured pays out‑of‑pocket before the insurer pays.
Applies to collision and comprehensive claims.
Higher deductible → lower premium (more risk on insured).
Insurer pays = Loss − Deductible (if loss > deductible).

cards.front: Collision damage \$3,200, deductible \$500. How much does the insurer pay?
back: Insured pays the first \$500.

cards.front: List four factors that affect [[kw:auto insurance premiums]].
back: Age and gender (younger drivers pay more; males higher).
Driving record (accidents and tickets increase premiums).
Location (urban areas have higher rates due to traffic and theft).
Vehicle type (expensive, high‑performance cars cost more to insure).
Coverage limits (higher limits = higher premiums).
Deductible (higher deductible = lower premium).

cards.front: Your car has ACV \$12,000, collision deductible \$500, and is totaled. How much does your insurer pay?
back: Insurer pays ACV − deductible = \$12,000 − \$500 = \$11,500.
If you owe more on a loan, gap insurance would cover the difference.
Common stock: gives voting rights; dividends vary; higher potential gains.
Preferred stock: usually no voting rights; priority in dividends and assets; fixed dividend rate.
Cumulative preferred requires all past missed dividends (arrears) to be paid before common dividends.
cards.front: Define [[kw:common stock]] and [[kw:preferred stock]].
What are [[kw:dividends in arrears]]?
back: Unpaid past dividends on cumulative preferred stock.
Must be paid before common stockholders receive any dividends.
Example: \$2.00 preferred dividend missed last year → \$2.00 per share in arrears.

cards.front: How do you calculate [[kw:stock yield]]?
back: $$\text{Stock Yield} = \frac{\text{Annual Dividend per Share}}{\text{Last Price per Share}} \times 100$$
Based on the closing price, not your purchase price.
Example: \$1.20 dividend, \$40 price → yield = 3\%.
Price‑Earnings ratio: $$\text{PE Ratio} = \frac{\text{Last Price per Share}}{\text{Annual Earnings per Share}}$$
Shows how much investors pay per dollar of earnings.
High PE → growth expectations; low PE may indicate undervaluation.
cards.front: What is the [[kw:PE ratio]] and how is it computed?

back: 1. Pay any dividends in arrears on cumulative preferred.
2. Pay current year's preferred dividend.
3. Remaining amount goes to common stockholders.
[[imp:Common gets nothing until preferred claims are fully satisfied.]]
cards.front: Explain the order of dividend payments when cumulative preferred stock exists.

back: Total Cost = Shares × Purchase Price + Buy Commission.
Total Return = (Selling Price − Purchase Price) × Shares + Dividends − Commissions.
$$\text{ROI} = \frac{\text{Total Return}}{\text{Total Cost}} \times 100$$
[[imp:Always include commissions in both cost and proceeds.]]
cards.front: How is [[kw:return on investment (ROI)]] for a stock calculated?
Buy 100 shares at \$30, sell at \$35. Commissions \$15 each. No dividends. Find ROI.
What is a [[kw:bond]]?
back: A long‑term debt instrument issued by corporations or governments.
Bondholders are creditors, not owners; they receive interest, not dividends.
Pay regular interest and return the [[kw:face value]] at maturity (usually \$1,000).
Interest = Face Value × Coupon Rate.
Quoted as a percent of face value (e.g., 102.5 = 102.5\% of face).
Market Price = Face × (Quoted Price / 100).
Current Yield = Annual Interest ÷ Market Price × 100.
Current yield reflects the return based on what you actually pay.
cards.front: How are [[kw:bond prices]] quoted and what is the [[kw:current yield]]?

back: Coupon > market rate → bond sells at a premium (above face).
Coupon < market rate → bond sells at a discount (below face).
Coupon = market rate → bond sells at par.
[[imp:Bond prices move inversely to market interest rates.]]
cards.front: Explain the relationship between coupon rate and bond pricing.

back: Interest = \$60.
Price < face → discount bond.
Current yield > coupon rate because of the discount.
cards.front: A \$1,000 bond with a 6\% coupon is bought for \$920. Find current yield and classify.

back: A professionally managed investment that pools money from many investors to buy a diversified portfolio.
NAV per share = (Total Assets − Total Liabilities) ÷ Shares Outstanding.
NAV is computed daily; it's the value of one share of the fund.
Mutual funds offer diversification and professional management.
cards.front: What is a [[kw:mutual fund]] and its [[kw:net asset value (NAV)]]?
Calculate NAV: assets \$500 million, liabilities \$20 million, shares 12 million.

back: A sales charge added to the purchase price (front‑end) or deducted when shares are sold (back‑end).
Public offering price (POP) = NAV ÷ (1 − Load\% as decimal).
No‑load funds have no sales charge.
[[imp:The load is a percentage of the POP, not the NAV.]]
cards.front: What is a [[kw:load]] in a mutual fund and how does it affect the purchase price?

back: Investors pay \$31.25 per share; the fund receives \$30.00.
cards.front: NAV \$30, load 4\%. Find POP.

back: The annual fee expressed as a percentage of the fund's average net assets.
Covers management fees, administrative costs, and 12b‑1 marketing fees.
Deducted from the fund's assets daily, lowering the NAV.
[[imp:Applies to all funds, including no‑load. Lower is better for long‑term returns.]]
cards.front: What is an [[kw:expense ratio]] in a mutual fund?

back: The arithmetic average of a set of numbers.
$$\text{Mean} = \frac{\text{Sum of all values}}{\text{Number of values}}$$
Sensitive to extreme values (outliers).
cards.front: Define the [[kw:mean]] and give its formula.
Find the mean of: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50.
back: Number of values = 5.
An average where each value is multiplied by its frequency (weight) before summing.
$$\text{Weighted Mean} = \frac{\sum (x_i \times f_i)}{\sum f_i}$$
Example: GPA—grade points weighted by credit hours.
cards.front: Define the [[kw:weighted mean]] and give an example.
Define the [[kw:median]] and how to find it.
back: The middle value when data are ordered from smallest to largest.
Odd count: middle number; even count: average of the two middle numbers.
Not affected by extreme values—better for skewed data (e.g., incomes, home prices).

cards.front: Find the median of: \$27k, \$32k, \$40k, \$67k, \$95k.
back: Ordered: 27k, 32k, 40k, 67k, 95k.
5 values → 3rd is median = \$40k.

cards.front: Define the [[kw:mode]] and when it is most useful.
back: The value that appears most frequently in a data set.
Can be one mode, multiple modes (bimodal), or no mode.
Best for categorical data or finding the most popular item (e.g., shoe size, color).

cards.front: What is a [[kw:frequency distribution]]?
back: A table that groups data into classes (intervals) and shows the count (frequency) in each class.
Steps: Find range (max−min), choose number of classes, compute class width (range ÷ classes, round up), tally data.
Used to summarize large datasets and reveal patterns.
Uses rectangular bars of equal width separated by spaces.
Categories on x‑axis; frequencies/values on y‑axis.
Best for comparing distinct categories at one point in time.
[[imp:Vertical axis must start at zero to avoid misleading visuals.]]
cards.front: Describe a [[kw:bar graph]] and its appropriate use.

back: Plots data points connected by lines, showing trends over time.
Time on x‑axis, variable on y‑axis.
Best for time‑series data (monthly sales, yearly profit).
Multiple lines can compare trends.
cards.front: Explain a [[kw:line graph]] and when to use it.

back: Divides a circle into slices proportional to category percentages of the whole.
$$\text{Slice Angle} = \text{Percent} \times 3.6°$$
Used to show parts‑of‑a‑whole (budget, market share).
[[imp:Total must equal 100%; limit slices for clarity.]]
cards.front: What is a [[kw:circle graph]] (pie chart) and how do you compute slice angles?
Define [[kw:price relative]] and its formula.
back: Compares the current price of an item to its price in a base period.
$$\text{Price Relative} = \frac{\text{Current Price}}{\text{Base Price}} \times 100$$
Above 100 = increase; below 100 = decrease.

cards.front: Calculate price relative: base price \$4.00, current price \$5.00.
back: Prices increased 25% from the base period.

cards.front: Define the [[kw:range]] in a dataset.
back: The difference between the maximum and minimum values.
$$\text{Range} = \text{Max} - \text{Min}$$
Simple but only uses two values; heavily influenced by outliers.

cards.front: What is the [[kw:standard deviation]] and how is it calculated for a sample?
back: Measures the average distance of data points from the mean.
Sample formula: $$s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n-1}}$$
Larger SD = more variability; smaller SD = data clustered closer to mean.
Use n−1 for samples to obtain an unbiased estimate.
For normal (bell‑shaped) distributions:
~68% of data lie within ±1 SD of the mean.
~95% within ±2 SD.
~99.7% within ±3 SD.
Useful for detecting outliers and understanding data spread.
[[imp:Only valid for approximately normal distributions.]]
cards.front: Explain the [[kw:empirical rule]] (68‑95‑99.7 rule).

back: A relative measure of variability expressed as a percentage of the mean.
$$\text{CV} = \frac{\text{SD}}{\text{Mean}} \times 100$$
Unitless – ideal for comparing variability across datasets with different means or units.
Lower CV indicates greater consistency.
cards.front: What is the [[kw:coefficient of variation (CV)]]?

back: Machine A is more consistent (lower CV).
cards.front: Machine A: mean 50, SD 2. Machine B: mean 30, SD 1.5. Which is more consistent?
